newsitem.title: USA: Slovenia PM lobbies Clinton on NATO from carrier.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM lobbies Clinton on NATO from carrier.
newsitem.dateline: ABOARD THE USS JOHN F. KENNEDY 1997-06-22

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek on Sunday visited a U.S. aircraft carrier in the Adriatic, from where he wired U.S. President Bill Clinton in a last-ditch bid for NATO entry in the first round of expansion.

"May this visit be yet another contribution ... paving the way to full integration of Slovenia in the Euroatlantic community," Drnovsek said in a telegram sent to Clinton from the carrier USS John F. Kennedy.
Drnovsek arrived by U.S. navy plane, one of 74 on the carrier. Among his party were Slovenian Defence Minister Tit Turnsek and U.S. Ambassador to Slovenia Victor Jackovich.
During the three-hour visit the guests were given a demonstration of fighter jets taking off and landing at 45-second intervals on two narrow runways.
The carrier is the second largest in the U.S. fleet and is part of the U.S. peace-keeping mission to Bosnia.

Earlier this month Washington dashed the hopes of Romania and Slovenia when it announced that only the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary should be included in the first wave of countries to join NATO.

Italy and France, the main backers of the Slovenia and Romania's candidacy say they should be included to ensure a balance between NATO's northern and southern flanks and show the alliance's concern for security in the Balkans.
Drnovsek said last week that the former Yugoslav republic would continue its efforts to join in spite of the U.S. decision.
"Our chances for inclusion are very small but they still exist," he said. "Some NATO members said a last-minute compromise was possible," he added.

The carrier, with a crew of 4,700 men, is due to arrive at Slovenia's port Koper on Monday morning where it will stay for three days and take part in the celebrations of the country's sixth independence anniversary on June 25.
Drnovsek's visit comes just 16 days ahead of NATO's summit in Madrid where the alliance will formally decide which former communist countries to invite to apply for membership.
